# Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels of Knowledge-Graph Tool Use

Tianda Sun Affiliation: University of York Affiliation: Department of
Computer Science Affiliation: Heslington, York Affiliation: YO10 5DD
Email: [tianda.sun@york.ac.uk](mailto:)    Dimitar Kazakov
Affiliation: University of York Affiliation: Department of Computer
Science Affiliation: Heslington, York Affiliation: YO10 5DD
Email: [dimitar.kazakov@york.ac.uk](mailto:)

###### Abstract

We test the standard RLVR tool-use recipe (GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)
on a deliberately minimal knowledge-graph tool API: four Freebase
navigation verbs over Complex WebQuestions. Under a self-verifiable
retrieval reward (R-selfV), the policy’s correct-via-tool rate climbs
from $`3.8\%`$ to $`9.6\%`$ over 250 steps, then collapses to $`0\%`$
within a single 50-step window, a _peak-then-collapse_ pattern
replicated across four seeds. Over the same window, strict EM falls
$`39.5{\to}0.0\%`$ and containment EM falls $`46.1{\to}12.1\%`$. Across
seven reward designs, we find four recurring failure modes: adding
denser or more targeted proxy rewards shifts the failure mode rather
than eliminating it. We argue that a key difference from Python
interpreters, web search, and JSON APIs is interface feedback: their
failures often leak natural-language signal the model saw in
pretraining. A Python traceback names the failing line; an empty
Freebase result \[\] does not. Within the seven-design ladder, stripping
away that surface exposes a degradation regime not removed by the
same-family redesigns. Full-test relation- and entity-replacement
oracles change EM by only $`+0.20`$ and $`+0.42`$ pp, and $`95.4\%`$ of
retrieval-dependent errors are retrieval-composition rather than
answer-extraction failures. As mitigation, one-iteration
self-distillation reaches $`40.0\%`$ EM at 7B; a differently configured
14B run reaches $`40.2\%`$, so this comparison does not isolate
capacity.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models increasingly act as _agents_: they call external
tools (code interpreters, web search, function APIs) and are trained to
use them by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where
a checkable outcome (did the code run? did the answer match?) supplies
the reward ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Qian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)). The dominant recipe (dense process rewards,
GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), a 7B-scale policy) is treated as
portable across tool families. We test that portability on a knowledge
graph (KG), whose interface is by construction the opposite of the
pretraining-aligned surfaces RLVR usually enjoys. Our benchmark is
Complex WebQuestions (CWQ) ([Talmor and Berant, 2018](#bib.bib19)), a
standard multi-hop question-answering task over the Freebase ([Bollacker
et al., 2008](#bib.bib20)) knowledge graph, which we re-cast from its
usual gold-subgraph/SPARQL form into a _deliberately minimal tool-use
interface_: the policy must reach answers by composing four navigation
verbs (the outgoing or incoming relations of an entity, and the entities
reachable from it along a relation), where every entity is an opaque
machine ID (m.0d3k14) and every miss returns an uninformative empty
list. Python tool use leaks natural-language signal the model saw in
pretraining (a traceback names the failing line), whereas this KG
interface leaks almost none. We ask whether the standard RLVR-tool
recipe still converges once that surface is removed.

Across seven reward designs trained on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ([Qwen,
2024](#bib.bib18)) + CWQ, we find four distinct failure modes, none
solved by the next reward design in the same family. The signature
finding is a Qwen/R-selfV _peak-then-collapse_
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")):
a self-verifiable retrieval reward (one that checks whether a returned
entity appears verbatim in the answer, gold-free) lifts _grounded
retrieval_ (the correct-via-tool rate, CvT) from $`3.8\%`$ to $`9.6\%`$
over 250 training steps, then collapses to $`0\%`$ in a single 50-step
window across four seeds. In that window, strict EM falls
$`39.5{\to}0.0\%`$ and containment EM (ContEM) falls $`46.1{\to}12.1\%`$
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

Agentic-RL collapse phenomena have been documented ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)), but at the level of action-distribution entropy and
reward variance. The specific mechanism we observe, a one-shot
quote-and-stop attractor with mean tool calls per question (Tools/Q)
dropping $`3.0{\to}1.0`$ in a 50-step window, is a call-volume signature
distinct from these precedents and from the standard RLHF reward-hacking
framework ([Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Pan et al.,
2022](#bib.bib31); [Skalse et al., 2022](#bib.bib32)), which reports
proxy-overoptimisation at the level of learned reward models. Across the
seven-design ladder, stripping away the pretraining-aligned surface
exposes a degradation regime not removed by the same-family redesigns in
the main experiment.

Figure 1: Peak-then-collapse for Qwen2.5-7B under R-selfV. Top: CvT
(correct-via-tool rate; left, blue) climbs $`3.77{\to}9.57\%`$ (steps
0–250) then falls to $`0`$ by step 300; strict EM falls
$`39.51{\to}0.00\%`$ while ContEM falls $`46.13{\to}12.14\%`$. Bottom:
Tools/Q drops $`3.0{\to}1.0`$ across the shaded 50-step window.
self-distill (dashed) reaches $`40.0\%`$ EM / $`5.81\%`$ CvT in the same
reward family. Mechanism:
§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").

We run a controlled comparison: one primary model, one task, one
algorithm (GRPO), one tool API (the 4-verb Freebase interface), and
seven reward designs read as a pragmatic ladder
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Reward ladder ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use");
two rungs also vary the KL tether or initialisation). To explain the
convergent failures, we formalise the tool-API-to-policy-gradient
pathway as four channels along which a tool API supplies (or fails to
supply) RL signal: silent failure, symbolic schema, opaque compositional
state, and absent pretraining prior
($`L_{\mathrm{sig/lang/comp/prior}}`$). We use the channels to organise
the observed failure surfaces
(§[5](#S5 "5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
At the strongest in-family checkpoint, replacing relation arguments with
gold relations changes EM by only $`+0.20`$ pp; a complementary
entity-replacement oracle changes it by $`+0.42`$ pp. Together with the
error decomposition, these results point to joint retrieval-composition
failures.

#### Contributions.

(C1) A controlled comparison of seven reward designs on a single primary
model $`\times`$ task $`\times`$ algorithm $`\times`$ tool API,
organised into a four-mode failure taxonomy
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
(C2) A signal-theoretic four-channel framework supported by relation-
and entity-replacement oracles, plus a step-level error decomposition
where $`95.4\%`$ of $`1{,}958`$ _retrieval-dependent_ errors localise to
retrieval composition rather than answer extraction
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Mechanism evidence chain ‣ 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
(C3) A one-iteration ReST-EM-style self-distillation recipe reaching
EM=$`40.0\%`$ at 7B; the 5K rule-based pre-SFT prefix is dispensable. A
differently configured 14B run reaches $`40.2\%`$
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested 40% band ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
(C4) Step-resolved (50-step cadence, full CWQ test set) Qwen/R-selfV
peak-then-collapse across four seeds: a call-volume signature (Tools/Q
$`3.0{\to}1.0`$) novel relative to the action-distribution entropy and
reward-variance diagnostics of prior agentic-RL collapse ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26))
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

We release all code, reward implementations, per-checkpoint evaluations,
and the seven-category trajectory classifier at
[https://github.com/TiandaSun/KG_GRPO](https://github.com/TiandaSun/KG_GRPO).

## 2 Related Work

#### Process-reward RL for tools and knowledge graphs.

Process-reward recipes for tool-using LLMs ([Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Qian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)) succeed on tool APIs
with pretraining-aligned surfaces; we test whether the same recipe
transfers to KG tools deliberately stripped of natural-language surface.
KG-specific variants using KGs to _define_ rewards (fs1 ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib10)); HyperGraphPro ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib8));
KG-Implicit-RM ([Kansal and Jha, 2026](#bib.bib9))) differ from our
setup, which uses the KG to evaluate the policy (under RoG’s ([Luo et
al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) subgraph filter; strict EM motivated by [Zhang
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14)). On the same Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct + CWQ
benchmark, richer-pipeline concurrent systems report higher numbers
while changing several components (GraphWalker ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)) adds $`\sim 21`$K-trajectory SFT + BM25 + an LLM
reranker, $`79.6\%`$ EM; Graph-RFT ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib24))
adds web fallback over a $`40\%`$-incomplete KG, $`67.2\%`$ Hits@1).
These cross-system comparisons motivate studying interface enrichment,
but do not isolate it from data, training, or evaluation differences.
Our stripped-interface diagnostic is a deliberate complement.

#### Cold-start SFT-then-RL.

Our self-distillation recipe sits in the cold-start-SFT-then-RL
family ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib3);
[Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)); the methodological extension is that
our SFT corpus is _self-distilled_ from our own RL checkpoint with a
strict EM-correct $`\cap`$ tool-productive $`\cap`$ format-valid filter,
connecting to ReST-EM ([Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)). The
no-rule-prefix variant
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested 40% band ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
shows that removing the rule-SFT prefix while retaining
self-distillation SFT reaches the same approximately $`40\%`$ EM band,
consistent with ReST-EM’s init-from-base prescription on a different
task family.

#### Reward hacking and agentic-RL collapse.

The peak-then-collapse mode
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
extends a known reward-hacking pattern. RLHF ([Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32); [Pan et al., 2022](#bib.bib31); [Gao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30)) catalogues proxy-overoptimisation at the
learned-reward-model level; agentic-RL diagnostics include
action-distribution entropy ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), reward
variance (Echo Trap [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib25); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), and
metric-without-capability gain ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib28))
(closely related to our R-stepwise tool-free shortcut,
§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2 "Mode 2: Verify-Then-Answer Goodhart (R-stepwise). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"));
[Yue et al. (2025)](#bib.bib29) (RL on math does not push pass@$`k`$
beyond base) is our closest non-KG analogue. Our peak-then-collapse
contribution is the Tools/Q call-volume signature ($`3.0{\to}1.0`$) and
step-resolved cadence on a KG-tool agent.

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 Task and KG tool interface

We use Complex WebQuestions (CWQ) ([Talmor and Berant,
2018](#bib.bib19)) over Freebase ([Bollacker et al., 2008](#bib.bib20)),
following the standard RoG ([Luo et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) splits
($`27{,}639`$ train / $`3{,}531`$ test).¹¹ 1 $`27{,}639`$ is RoG’s
row-expanded count over (question, gold-path) pairs; the canonical
rmanluo/RoG-cwq release reports $`16{,}894`$ unique training questions.
Talmor & Berant’s original v1.1 release uses $`27{,}734`$ / $`3{,}480`$
/ $`3{,}475`$; the residual differences are Freebase-reachability
filtering. Answers are normalised (lowercase, strip articles, strip
punctuation, whitespace-collapse) before exact-match scoring. The RoG
subgraph filter yields $`2.59`$M entities, $`7{,}058`$ relations,
$`8.3`$M triples accessible at inference time.

The model accesses the KG through a _four-verb_ tool interface:

- •
  get_tail_relations(e), get_head_relations(e): list relations outgoing
  from / incoming into entity $`e`$.
- •
  get_tail_entities(e, r), get_head_entities(e, r): list entities
  reachable from $`e`$ along relation $`r`$ in either direction.

Tool calls are emitted as \<search\>verb(args)\</search\> tokens; the KG
response is inlined verbatim into the context and generation continues.
Up to five tool-calling turns are permitted per question. The interface
is deliberately minimal: four verbs, one symbol per query, responses
that list entities or relations line-by-line. Unlike a web-search RAG
surface, every query response can be objectively classified as
successful, empty, or off-schema, the property that makes step-resolved
reward analysis tractable.
Figure [7](#A5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ E.1 Setup: standard multi-hop KGQA re-cast as a minimal tool interface ‣ Appendix E Framework illustration and per-claim caveats ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
(App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Framework illustration and per-claim caveats ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
illustrates the re-cast.

### 3.2 Shared SFT initialisation

All reward-family ablations share a single SFT-initialised
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ([Qwen, 2024](#bib.bib18)) checkpoint with LoRA
($`r{=}64`$, $`\alpha{=}128`$, DoRA + rslora) on $`5{,}000`$ rule-based
trajectories whose \<search\> calls are constructed _from the gold
triple chain_ (no LLM teacher: no GPT-4, no Claude, no Qwen-72B
distillation). The rule-based generator and the $`14{,}082`$-trajectory
G-variant corpus are in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C SFT corpora ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").
A Qwen2.5-14B configuration
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 The reward-ladder matrix ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
and a Llama-3.1-8B-Base boundary check
(App. [F](#A6 "Appendix F Cross-family boundary check: Llama-3.1-8B-Base ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
use model-specific SFT pre-warms and different reward protocols, probing
configuration and model-family boundaries around the primary
Qwen/R-selfV setting.

### 3.3 GRPO training

GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)) on the SFT base: group size
$`8`$, low_var_kl loss, KL coefficient $`0.05`$ unless noted
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 The reward-ladder matrix ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
for per-variant overrides), lr $`3\mathrm{e}{-7}`$, batch $`128`$,
$`500`$ steps; verl ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)) + vLLM ([Kwon et
al., 2023](#bib.bib22)) rollouts on NVIDIA GH200. Reward implementations
are unit-tested ($`18/18`$ passing;
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

### 3.4 Reward ladder

Intuitively, the ladder first tests whether final-answer reward alone
preserves the tool format, then adds verifiable tool-call structure,
then rewards productive tool use, then stabilises the policy with a
stronger KL tether. R-selfV tests whether a gold-free retrieved-entity
signal can improve grounding, while self-distill tests whether
successful trajectories can stabilise the best in-family policy.
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.4 Reward ladder ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
summarises the six-rung design.

| Rung | Name             | Patch over predecessor                                       | EM                 | CvT                 | Mode emerged       |
| ---- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------ |
| 1    | R-binary         | $`r_{\mathrm{out}}`$ only                                    | $`0.000`$          | —                   | Mode 1 (format)    |
| 2    | R-stepwise       | $`+\,r_{\mathrm{valid}}+r_{\mathrm{path}}+r_{\mathrm{coh}}`$ | $`0.325`$          | $`0.03\%`$          | Mode 2 (ritual)    |
| 3    | R-toolverbs      | $`+\,r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}type}}`$ bonus                   | $`0.322`$          | $`3.03\%`$          | Mode 3 (drift)     |
| 4    | R-toolverbs·KL   | KL $`\times 5`$ (SFT-prior tether)                           | $`0.384`$          | $`3.77\%`$          | stable to $`400+`$ |
| 5    | R-selfV^(⋆)      | $`+\,r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ (entity in answer)                 | $`0.395`$          | $`\mathbf{9.57\%}`$ | Mode 4 (cliff)     |
| 6    | self-distill^(⋆) | R-toolverbs + self-distilled SFT pre-warm                    | $`\mathbf{0.400}`$ | $`5.81\%`$          | stable (best EM)   |

We organise reward design as a six-rung ladder
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.4 Reward ladder ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"));
each rung is introduced as a patch for a specific named failure of its
predecessor (failure modes in
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use");
full reward formulas in
App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
Rungs 4 and 6 also vary non-reward ingredients (KL coefficient;
initialisation/data regime), so we read the ladder _pragmatically_ (does
each patch fix its predecessor’s failure?) rather than as strictly
single-variable reward ablations.²² 2 Three earlier variants (E2
heuristic, E4 random-reward control, E5a retrieval-grounded cold-start)
were run but cut as redundant; see
App. [B.6](#A2.SS6 "B.6 Cut variants and rationale ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").
(1) R-binary: outcome-only $`r{=}0.5\,\mathrm{EM}{+}0.5\,\mathrm{F1}`$
(Search-R1 ([Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)),
DeepSeek-R1-zero ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib16)) family). (2)
R-stepwise: equal-weight
$`r_{\mathrm{out}}{+}r_{\mathrm{valid}}{+}r_{\mathrm{path}}{+}r_{\mathrm{coh}}`$
($`r_{\mathrm{valid}}`$ checks call syntax, $`r_{\mathrm{path}}`$
rewards gold-relation queries, $`r_{\mathrm{coh}}`$ scores
\<think\>-vs-call coherence; KG analogue of StepSearch ([Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2))). (3) R-toolverbs:
$`r{=}0.25\,r_{\mathrm{out}}{+}0.50\,r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}type}}{+}0.25\,r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}usage}}`$,
rewarding all 4 verbs and non-empty responses (no gold supervision). (4)
R-toolverbs·KL: R-toolverbs with KL coef raised $`5{\times}`$
($`0.05{\to}0.25`$); extends R-toolverbs’s stable window
step 150$`\to`$400+. (5) R-selfV:
$`r{=}0.25\,r_{\mathrm{ans}}{+}0.50\,r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}type}}{+}0.25\,r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$,
$`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}{=}|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{prod}}|/|\mathcal{T}|`$
where $`t{\in}\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{prod}}`$ iff response non-empty and
$`\geq`$1 returned KG entity appears verbatim in \<answer\>. Gold-free
at GRPO training. (6) self-distill: roll out R-toolverbs·KL@400
greedily, filter EM-correct/tool-productive/format-valid trajectories
($`14{,}082`$, $`50.9\%`$ yield), SFT from base, then R-toolverbs GRPO.

init-from-base ablation
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested 40% band ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
drops the 5K rule-based pre-SFT prefix and reaches the same
approximately $`40\%`$ EM band.

### 3.5 Evaluation

Unless otherwise noted, numbers are reported on the full 3,531-question
CWQ test set with greedy decoding, max_new_tokens=512, and up to five
tool-calling turns; pass@$`k`$ and the closed-model control instead use
the smaller subsets and sampling temperatures noted inline.

#### Held-out checkpoint-selection check.

Because the body checkpoint labels were initially selected from
full-test monitoring, we assess their sensitivity with a hop-stratified
dev split ($`n{=}800`$, seed 42) and re-select every reported checkpoint
on dev alone. The dev peak is step 250 (matching the body), and held-out
test EM ($`n{=}2{,}731`$) lies within the Wilson 95% half-width
($`\pm 1.85`$ pp) of full-set EM for all ten checkpoints
(App. [B.10](#A2.SS10 "B.10 Held-out dev/test checkpoint-selection robustness ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

#### Scalar metrics.

- •
  EM: exact match after normalisation.
- •
  CvT, the _correct-via-tool_ rate: EM-correct _and_ $`\geq 1`$ returned
  KG entity appears verbatim in the final \<answer\>.
- •
  ContEM, _containment_ EM: gold answer is contained as a substring of
  the normalised prediction (looser than EM; reported for closed-model
  controls where strict gold-form normalisation is lossy, e.g., GPT-4o
  in
  App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D GPT-4o closed-model schema-unfamiliarity control ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"),
  and for collapse-trajectory diagnostics, e.g.,
  Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
- •
  hard-partition CvT: CvT restricted to the Cat B subset
  ($`n{=}2{,}556`$ structurally-hard questions; pass@10$`=`$0 on base
  Qwen;
  App. [B.8](#A2.SS8 "B.8 Cat A / Cat B stratified results ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
- •
  Tools/Q: mean number of \<search\> calls per question.

#### Seven-category trajectory classification.

Every trajectory is assigned exactly one of: correct-via-tool /
correct-via-memory / correct-no-tool / wrong-no-tool / kg-incomplete /
tool-misuse / wrong-answer; full definitions + decision tree in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").

#### Statistics.

Confidence intervals are Wilson 95% ([Wilson, 1927](#bib.bib33)); paired
comparisons use McNemar’s test ([McNemar, 1947](#bib.bib34)) (exact
binomial for $`n<25`$, continuity-corrected $`\chi^{2}`$ otherwise). For
pass@$`k`$
(§[4](#S4 "4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
we additionally evaluate 16 samples per question at temperature 1 on a
500-question seed-42 subset.

### 4.2 Pass@16: tools as decoration vs. capability extension

Figure 2: Pass@16 with vs. without tool access on a 500-Q seed-42 subset
(16 samples per question). R-stepwise’s gap is statistically zero
($`-0.4`$ pp): the policy has stopped using tools. R-toolverbs and
R-toolverbs·KL each show $`+11.4`$ to $`+14.2`$ pp of genuine tool-lift.
self-distill (EM-best) is measured separately
(App. [B.11](#A2.SS11 "B.11 Self-distill pass@16 tool-dependence ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")):
a $`+11.5`$ pp tool-lift confirms it genuinely consumes retrieval.

On 500 seed-42 questions $`\times`$ 16 samples, R-stepwise’s
with-vs-without-tools gap is statistically zero ($`-0.4`$ pp;
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Pass@16: tools as decoration vs. capability extension ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")),
while R-toolverbs@100 and R-toolverbs·KL@400 show $`+14.2`$ and
$`+11.4`$ pp; the EM-best self-distill shows a genuine $`+11.5`$ pp lift
on a separate subset
(App. [B.11](#A2.SS11 "B.11 Self-distill pass@16 tool-dependence ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
The gap distinguishes ritualistic from capability-extending tool use,
complementing [Yue et al. (2025)](#bib.bib29) (RL does not push
pass@$`k`$ beyond the base model): process rewards shift the answer
source from parametric memory to retrieval consumption.

### 4.3 Four failure modes

The seven reward designs produce four distinct failure modes, differing
in _what fails_: format, tool-use ritual, format-after-tool-use, or the
signal the reward optimises. Each successive design _shifts_ the failure
rather than eliminating it. Mode 4 (peak-then-collapse) is the strongest
expression of this pattern and we give its mechanism in full here;
Modes 1–3 follow the same shift-not-eliminate dynamic and are summarised
below, with full mechanism prose in
App. [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Failure-mode mechanism details (Modes 1–3) ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").
The seven-category trajectory classifier
(App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use");
exemplars in
App. [G](#A7 "Appendix G Trajectory exemplars ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
labels every test-set trajectory.

#### Mode 1: Sparse-Reward Format Collapse (R-binary, R-binary-SR).

Both reach EM=$`0.000`$ at format-valid $`0/3531`$. Outcome-only reward
fires only on EM-match; early exploration supplies little signal before
low-entropy degeneracy locks in. R-binary-SR (Search-R1’s kl_coef=0.001
configuration;
App. [A](#A1 "Appendix A Search-R1 reimplementation rationale ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
also collapses, demonstrating sparse-reward format collapse across two
hyperparameter regimes.

#### Mode 2: Verify-Then-Answer Goodhart (R-stepwise).

R-stepwise reaches EM=$`32.5\%`$ but CvT=$`0.03\%`$ ($`1/3531`$):
Tools/Q=$`1.0`$ with $`100\%`$ of calls hitting get_tail_relations (the
only verb that never returns empty). The 4-component verifiable-step
reward incentivises structural existence checks over tool-output
consumption, a tool-free shortcut (component-gaming Goodhart, cf. [Gao
et al., 2023](#bib.bib30)). The Pass@16 with-vs-without-tools gap of
$`-0.4`$ pp
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Pass@16: tools as decoration vs. capability extension ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
confirms tools are decorative.

#### Mode 3: Format Drift Collapse (R-toolverbs, late stage).

R-toolverbs briefly succeeds at step 100 (EM=$`32.2\%`$, CvT=$`3.03\%`$,
Tools/Q=$`2.30`$, the first reward with non-trivial grounded retrieval)
but by step 150 \<search\> tags drift inside \<think\> tags; by step 200
calls fail to parse; by step 250 strict EM approaches $`0\%`$.
R-toolverbs rewards tool-type diversity but anchors no output format;
format conventions drift from the SFT prior under loose KL. Raising KL
$`5{\times}`$ ($`0.05{\to}0.25`$) extends the stable window to
step 400+. A non-monotonic fixed-reward KL sweep points to an
interaction between tether strength and the limited corrective signal
after malformed calls
(App. [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Failure-mode mechanism details (Modes 1–3) ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

#### Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV).

R-selfV, the R-toolverbs reward augmented with a self-verifiable
retrieval-contribution term (a returned KG entity must appear verbatim
in the answer; full reward in
App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")),
exhibits the most distinctive trajectory and is the paper’s signature
finding.

_Climb._ Initialised from R-toolverbs·KL@400 (CvT=3.77%), CvT climbs
monotonically across five 50-step windows:
$`3.77\to 4.84\to 6.37\to 7.28\to 8.16\to 9.57\%`$ (peak at step 250;
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"),
top). EM moves in lockstep at low amplitude ($`0.384\to 0.395`$). Mean
Tools/Q is steady at 3.00, so the gain is a query-precision improvement
at constant call volume. Across four Qwen/R-selfV seeds, the peak occurs
at steps 200–250 and strict EM reaches $`0`$ by step 300.

_Cliff._ Between checkpoints 250 and 300 (a single 50-step window), the
policy collapses: EM $`0.3951\to 0.0000`$, ContEM
$`46.13\%\to 12.14\%`$, Tools/Q $`3.00\to 1.00`$
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"),
bottom). By step 400 ContEM is 6.30%; recovery does not occur. _No
training hyperparameter changes between step 250 and step 300_; the
collapse is entirely policy-internal.

_Mechanism (hypothesis)._ The retrieval-contribution term
$`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ fires whenever a returned entity appears verbatim
in the answer. Once the policy has learned to quote returned entities
(the productive climb), a _locally optimal degenerate_ strategy becomes
available: call any single tool, copy any entity from its response, emit
that entity as a terse answer, stop. This guarantees a productive call
at minimum sampling budget, maximising $`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ while
sacrificing EM. Two analyses support this reading
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Mode 4: Specification Gaming Cliff (R-selfV). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
First, per-checkpoint reward decomposition shows
$`r_{\mathrm{outcome}}`$ dies first ($`0.41\to 0.0007`$ across
step 250–300) while $`r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}type}}`$ and
$`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ _briefly saturate_ at $`\approx 0.51`$ at
step 300 (the per-call productivity denominator trivially hits 1.0 once
Tools/Q$`=1`$) before collapsing to $`\approx 0.09`$ by step 400.
Second, token-level entropy inside \<search\> tags drops
$`0.35\to 0.21`$ nats across step 200–400 while outside-tag entropy
stays at floor ($`\sim 0.01`$–$`0.04`$ nats), a _selective_ collapse on
the action subspace, complementing prior agentic-RL entropy
diagnostics ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)).

Figure 3: Mode 4 mechanism evidence. _Top:_ per-checkpoint reward
components (R-selfV; HPC seed-42). $`r_{\mathrm{out}}`$ dies in the
collapse window (shaded); $`r_{\mathrm{tool}}`$ and
$`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ briefly saturate at $`\approx 0.51`$ at step 300
(denominator gaming with Tools/Q$`=1`$) before themselves collapsing by
step 400. The weighted total $`r_{\mathrm{total}}`$ peaks
_post-collapse_ (step 300): specification-gaming Goodhart made visible.
_Bottom:_ token entropy in nats, partitioned by inside vs. outside
\<search\> spans. Inside-tag entropy drops $`0.35\to 0.21`$ across step
200–400; outside-tag entropy stays at floor, a selective action-subspace
collapse.

_Why this matters._ This proxy-overoptimisation shape is catalogued in
RLHF and agentic-RL ([Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib30); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)); our contribution is
the Tools/Q call-volume signature ($`3.0{\to}1.0`$) characterising it at
a behavioural level on a Qwen KG-tool agent
(§[2](#S2 "2 Related Work ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

### 4.4 Response-period diagnostic interventions

On 200-question diagnostics, replacing empty results with
natural-language error messages does not prevent the R-selfV cliff in
either of two seeds. In contrast, requiring two distinct non-empty calls
before $`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ can fire removes the baseline-time cliff
in three seeds through their available horizons (steps 300, 350, and
400). These diagnostics concern the Qwen/R-selfV transition rather than
the full-test performance level;
App. [B.12](#A2.SS12 "B.12 Response-period diagnostic interventions ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
reports the complete results and scope.

### 4.5 Trajectory composition

The seven-category breakdown (full table in
App. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Seven-category trajectory breakdown across the reward ladder ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
reveals two patterns. _kg-incomplete_ is the largest non-success bucket
for every rung-3-or-better checkpoint, falling monotonically across
rungs 3–6 ($`1{,}435\to 1{,}201\to 824\to 818`$) as the policy reaches
the KG more productively. The _wrong-answer_ bucket rises in lockstep:
retrieval-grounded but the answer is wrong.

### 4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested $`40\%`$ band

self-distill and self-distill (init-from-base) share an identical
$`14{,}082`$-trajectory self-distillation SFT (strict-filtered
R-toolverbs·KL@400 rollouts, $`50.9\%`$ yield) then R-toolverbs GRPO;
they differ only in whether a 5K rule-based gold-path pre-SFT prefix is
prepended (self-distill: yes; init-from-base: no, from raw base).
self-distill reaches EM=$`40.0\%`$, CvT=$`5.81\%`$ at step 500
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 The reward-ladder matrix ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use");
Tools/Q=$`3.00`$), replicated across four seeds (mean EM=$`40.21\%`$,
std $`0.46`$ pp); init-from-base matches at $`\approx 40\%`$ across
steps 100–500; the 5K rule-based prefix is dispensable in this setup.
self-distill (init-from-iterate) (no SFT; init from R-toolverbs·KL@400
iterate) reaches EM=$`39.4\%`$: the self-distillation SFT, not the
rule-based prefix, is the operative ingredient, consistent with
ReST-EM’s ([Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)) init-from-base
prescription.

### 4.7 External validity

Three controls probe simple alternatives. _(i) KG coverage_: bounded BFS
marks $`99.5\%`$ of CWQ and $`69.14\%`$ of KGQAGen-10k ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)) as 2-hop-solvable, both above the $`3`$–$`10\%`$ CvT
reached here. _(ii) Cross-benchmark_: 8 base Qwen variants give Spearman
$`\rho{=}0.976`$ between CWQ and KGQAGen-10k EM orderings, showing that
the two benchmarks preserve base-model ordering. _(iii) GPT-4o_: under
the same 4-verb interface, near-$`100\%`$ format-validity but only
$`6.2\%`$ ContEM and $`2.1\%`$ F1 on $`n{=}500`$ with $`\sim 78\%`$ of a
200-question subset self-reporting “unable to retrieve X”
(App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D GPT-4o closed-model schema-unfamiliarity control ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
The closed-model result independently illustrates schema unfamiliarity
on the stripped interface.

## 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty

The four failure modes characterised in
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
share a common substrate: each is a degradation of the gradient signal
GRPO needs to converge on a tool-grounded policy. We propose this
substrate has structure: four interface-level channels along which a
tool API supplies (or fails to supply) usable RL signal
(Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")),
yielding four channel-level claims. These channels are an organising
account of the observed failure surfaces and intervention points.

Figure 4: Synthesis: reward $`\to`$ failure mode $`\to`$ associated
interface channel. Each ladder rung
(§[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Reward ladder ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
produces a distinctive failure mode
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
with channel associations from
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Mechanism evidence chain ‣ 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use").
R-toolverbs$`\cdot`$KL is stable but plateaus at low CvT; self-distill
reaches the approximately $`40\%`$ EM band in the tested setup.

### 5.1 Four interface-level channels

Why do small ($`\leq`$7B) Qwen-class models learn Python ([Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), web-search ([Jin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), and JSON-API ([Qian et al., 2025](#bib.bib5))
tool use under similar GRPO recipes, yet struggle with compositional KG
tool use in our setting? Four structural properties of the interface
organise this contrast (diagram + tool-family table in
App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Framework illustration and per-claim caveats ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")):

- •
  $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ (silent failure). A KG miss returns \[\] with no
  information about _why_ (wrong entity, wrong relation, or both), in
  contrast to a Python traceback or HTTP 400 with named parameter. On
  our 7-reward matrix, $`\geq 99\%`$ of erroneous tool calls return
  identically \[\].
- •
  $`L_{\mathrm{lang}}`$ (symbolic schema). KG queries use opaque MIDs
  (m.0d3k14) and dotted relation names (people.person.place_of_birth),
  with little task-specific pretraining support relative to common
  programming or natural-language search surfaces.
- •
  $`L_{\mathrm{comp}}`$ (opaque compositional state). Multi-hop KG
  reasoning carries entity IDs across turns; these IDs are semantically
  opaque and any paraphrasing breaks the chain.
- •
  $`L_{\mathrm{prior}}`$ (weak pretraining prior). The policy has no
  demonstrated pretraining competence for Freebase schema navigation,
  unlike its documented exposure to common Python, search, and JSON
  patterns.

Matched canonical-name and unfamiliar-content variants would test
$`L_{\mathrm{lang}}`$ and $`L_{\mathrm{prior}}`$ more directly.

### 5.2 Four channel-level claims

We treat P1–P4
(Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Four channel-level claims ‣ 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
as joint _consistency checks_ of the descriptive structure (per-claim
caveats in
App. [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Per-claim caveats for P1–P4 ‣ Appendix E Framework illustration and per-claim caveats ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

| Claim                           | Evidence                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Reading                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| P1 Outcome-only collapse        | R-binary+R-binary-SR EM=$`0\%`$, format-valid $`0/3531`$ (Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 The reward-ladder matrix ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")) | confounds $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ with $`L_{\mathrm{prior}}`$ _(observational)_                |
| P2 Size and configuration check | 14B R-toolverbs$`\cdot`$KL vs. 7B self-distill hard-partition CvT $`4.61\%`$ vs. $`4.19\%`$                                                                                                                                                                     | both configurations remain in the same hard-partition CvT band _(configuration comparison)_ |
| P3 Self-distillation sufficient | raw-base and rule-SFT-prefixed both $`\approx 40\%`$ EM, $`\geq`$ init-from-iterate’s $`39.4\%`$                                                                                                                                                                | matches ReST-EM’s init-from-base _(ablation)_                                               |
| P4 Cross-benchmark ordering     | KGQAGen-10k Spearman $`\rho{=}0.976`$ on 8 base Qwen variants (§[4](#S4 "4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))                                             | base-model ordering is preserved across the two benchmarks _(cross-benchmark)_              |

type appears in _italics_.

### 5.3 Mechanism evidence chain

We characterise self-distill’s $`2{,}119`$ strict-EM=0 error
trajectories in two stages.

_Schema-surface failures are common._ A 4-channel attribution rubric on
these $`2{,}119`$ errors has $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ dominant at
$`55.2\%`$; a decision-boundary analysis
(App. [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Decision-boundary bucket distribution ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
finds $`70.4\%`$ of kg-incomplete first-search calls within
Lev$`\leq 1`$ of gold ($`4.7{\times}`$ null; held-out-unseen $`77.7\%`$
rules out memorisation), $`89.1\%`$ entity-correct/relation-wrong
($`90.4\%`$ same-entity-different-relation vs. R-toolverbs·KL).

_But relation selection alone is not the EM bottleneck._ We inject the
gold-chain relation at every \<search\> call while keeping the entity
argument and re-evaluate. This relation oracle changes EM by only
$`\mathbf{+0.20}`$ pp ($`40.19\%`$ vs. $`39.99\%`$), within the Wilson
95% CI half-width ($`\pm 1.6`$ pp at $`n{=}3{,}531`$). A complementary
entity oracle keeps policy relations but replaces the entity argument
with the edit-closest gold-chain entity; EM changes by
$`\mathbf{+0.42}`$ pp ($`40.41\%`$ vs. $`39.99\%`$) on the same full
test set. The entity oracle rewrites $`0.71`$ calls per trajectory
versus $`1.59`$ for the relation oracle. These marginal interventions do
not rule out joint entity–relation failures, but correcting either
argument alone is insufficient. Step-level classification of the
$`1{,}958`$ _retrieval-dependent_ errors
(Table [9](#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ B.9 Mechanism evidence chain (full table) ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
localises $`\mathbf{95.4\%}`$ to retrieval-composition failures versus
$`4.6\%`$ answer-extraction failures: the residual gap is upstream of
answer extraction.

A Llama-3.1-8B-Base boundary check
(App. [F](#A6 "Appendix F Cross-family boundary check: Llama-3.1-8B-Base ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
also fails to maintain tool-grounded behaviour, but via tool abandonment
(Tools/Q=$`0`$). Because it uses self-distill rather than R-selfV, it is
not a matched replication of the Qwen cliff.

## 6 Conclusion

Within a deliberately controlled scope (one primary model, one task, one
RL algorithm), seven GRPO-trained reward designs on
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct + CWQ reveal four interface-level failure modes
($`L_{\mathrm{sig/lang/comp/prior}}`$). Relation- and entity-replacement
oracles change EM by only $`+0.20`$ and $`+0.42`$ pp, and step-level
decomposition locates the residual gap upstream of answer extraction. A
one-iteration self-distillation recipe reaches $`40.0\%`$ EM at 7B; a
differently configured 14B run reaches $`40.2\%`$, so this comparison
does not isolate capacity. Methodologically, our 50-step cadence caught
the Qwen/R-selfV peak-then-collapse mode; step-resolved instrumentation
is essential for process-reward RL.

## Limitations

Our main experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, CWQ, GRPO, and one
stripped Freebase interface. The 14B and Llama experiments use different
reward protocols, so they are not matched tests of scale or model
family. We also do not evaluate a trained policy on a second benchmark.
The peak-then-collapse finding is therefore specific to Qwen/R-selfV in
this setting.

Per-step monitoring and final reporting use the full CWQ test set,
making checkpoint labels test-set-informed. A hop-stratified dev/test
re-selection recovers the reported checkpoints under one split
(App. [B.10](#A2.SS10 "B.10 Held-out dev/test checkpoint-selection robustness ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"));
future studies should reserve development data throughout.

## Appendix A Search-R1 reimplementation rationale

We re-implement the Search-R1 recipe using our verl pipeline:
outcome-only binary-EM reward (our outcome_em_only reward type,
unit-tested), Search-R1’s published hyperparameters
($`\texttt{kl\_coef}=0.001`$, $`\mathrm{lr}=10^{-6}`$, batch $`256`$,
$`500`$ steps). One configuration change to our pipeline, zero
dependency changes. We label this R-binary-SR throughout the paper and
treat it as a _reimplementation_, not a reproduction.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 The reward-ladder matrix ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
reports format-valid $`0/3531`$ and EM$`=0`$ for R-binary-SR at
convergence — a format-collapse outcome under outcome-only reward,
consistent with the sparse-reward format-collapse mechanism
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "Mode 1: Sparse-Reward Format Collapse (R-binary, R-binary-SR). ‣ 4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

## Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier

### B.1 Reward type definitions

All reward types are implemented in a shared verl_reward module with
$`18/18`$ unit tests passing. Notation: $`a`$ is the final \<answer\>
text after normalisation, $`y`$ is the gold answer, $`\mathcal{T}`$ is
the ordered sequence of \<search\> calls with their KG responses.

- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{EM}}(a,y)=\mathbf{1}[a=y]`$, $`r_{\mathrm{F1}}(a,y)`$
  token-overlap F1.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{out}}=0.5\,r_{\mathrm{EM}}+0.5\,r_{\mathrm{F1}}`$.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{valid}}`$: fraction of calls in $`\mathcal{T}`$ that
  parse as valid verb(args) matching the 4-verb schema.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{path}}`$:
  $`\mathbf{1}[\exists t\in\mathcal{T}:\mathrm{rel}(t)`$ on gold triple
  chain$`]`$.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{coh}}`$: sequence-match between \<think\> spans and their
  following \<search\> calls.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}type}}`$: number of distinct tool verbs
  covered in $`\mathcal{T}`$, scaled to $`[0,1]`$.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{tool\text{-}usage}}`$: fraction of calls in
  $`\mathcal{T}`$ with non-empty response.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ (I-Self):
  $`|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{prod}}|/|\mathcal{T}|`$, where
  $`t\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{prod}}`$ iff (i) the response is non-empty
  and (ii) at least one returned KG entity appears verbatim in $`a`$.
- •
  $`r_{\mathrm{ans}}`$ (I-Self): identical to $`r_{\mathrm{out}}`$ but
  with $`r_{\mathrm{EM}}`$ replaced by a length-normalised form that
  treats multi-token gold answers leniently.

### B.2 Seven-category trajectory classifier

For each trajectory $`\tau`$ on test question $`q`$ with gold answer
$`y`$, the classifier proceeds:

1.  1.  Parse $`\tau`$ into \<think\>, \<search\>, \<tool_response\>,
        \<answer\> spans.
2.  2.  If $`r_{\mathrm{EM}}(a,y)=1`$:
    - •
      if no \<search\> call: correct-no-tool;
    - •
      else if $`\exists t\in\mathcal{T}`$ with entity-in-answer:
      correct-via-tool;
    - •
      else: correct-via-memory.

3.  3.  Else (EM=0):
    - •
      if no \<search\> call: wrong-no-tool;
    - •
      if any \<search\> call parses invalid: tool-misuse;
    - •
      if all responses empty or disjoint from gold sub-graph:
      kg-incomplete;
    - •
      otherwise: wrong-answer.

Full implementation: scripts/task16_classify.py in the release bundle.
Edge cases (degenerate loops, overlong outputs, malformed \<answer\>
envelopes) are logged separately for manual audit.

### B.5 Failure-mode mechanism details (Modes 1–3)

Main body
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Four failure modes ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
presents Modes 1–3 in condensed form; full mechanism prose is preserved
here. Mode 4 (the signature peak-then-collapse finding) is presented in
full in the main body.

#### Mode 1: Sparse-Reward Format Collapse (R-binary, R-binary-SR).

R-binary (outcome-only) reaches strict EM=$`0.000`$, F1=$`0.119`$;
R-binary-SR at Search-R1’s exact hyperparameters (kl_coef=0.001,
lr=1e-6, batch=256) also collapses (strict EM=$`0.000`$, format-valid
$`0/3531`$, ContEM=$`36.45\%`$;
App. [A](#A1 "Appendix A Search-R1 reimplementation rationale ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
R-binary’s $`0\%`$ strict EM is a genuine format collapse, whereas
GPT-4o is near-$`100\%`$ format-valid with surface-form mismatch.
Outcome-only reward fires only on EM match, and early exploration
supplies little signal before low-entropy degeneracy locks in. The
second configuration demonstrates sparse-reward format collapse across
two hyperparameter regimes.

#### Mode 2: Verify-Then-Answer Goodhart (R-stepwise).

R-stepwise reaches EM=$`32.5\%`$ with CvT=$`0.03\%`$ ($`1/3531`$) — one
trajectory of $`3{,}531`$ actually grounds its answer in a tool
response. Tools/Q is $`1.0`$ and $`100\%`$ of those calls are
get_tail_relations, the only verb that never returns empty: tool calls
are ritualistic, the answer is generated from parametric memory.
Mechanism: the 4-component verifiable-step reward incentivises the
easier component (call a tool that satisfies a structural existence
check) over the harder one (consume the tool’s output) — a tool-free
shortcut (component-gaming Goodhart, cf. [Gao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30)); unlike RLHF proxy decorrelation, here the proxy-gold
correlation $`r{=}0.95`$–$`0.97`$ is _maintained_ throughout training.
Falsification via Pass@16 with-vs-without-tools: R-stepwise’s gap is
$`-0.4`$ pp
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 Pass@16: tools as decoration vs. capability extension ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
— even with 16 attempts and tool access the policy does not solve more
questions than parametric sampling; tools are decorative.

#### Mode 3: Format Drift Collapse (R-toolverbs, late stage).

R-toolverbs briefly succeeds: at step 100 the policy reaches
EM=$`32.2\%`$ with CvT=$`3.03\%`$ (Tools/Q=$`2.30`$) — the first reward
with non-trivial grounded retrieval. By step 150 \<search\> tags drift
inside \<think\> tags; by step 200 tool calls stop being parsed; by
step 250 strict EM approaches $`0\%`$ in a repetition loop. R-toolverbs
rewards tool-type diversity but anchors no output format; under the
loose-KL configuration, conventions drift from the SFT prior and the
executor stops parsing calls. Raising KL $`5\times`$ to $`0.25`$ extends
the stable window to step 400+. A fixed-reward KL sweep
($`\mathrm{kl}\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05,0.25\}`$) is non-monotonic,
pointing to an interaction between tether strength and the limited
corrective signal after malformed calls.

### B.10 Held-out dev/test checkpoint-selection robustness

To assess sensitivity to test-set-informed checkpoint selection
(§[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Evaluation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")),
we draw a hop-count-stratified split (seed 42) of the
$`3{,}531`$-question CWQ test set into a dev split ($`n{=}800`$) and a
held-out test split ($`n{=}2{,}731`$), re-select each reported
checkpoint on dev EM, and compare held-out test EM against the full-set
EM used in the body. At $`n{=}2{,}731`$, $`p{\approx}0.4`$, the Wilson
95% half-width is $`\pm 1.85`$ pp. The R-selfV dev-EM peak is step 250
(scanning $`\{200,250,300\}`$) — identical to the step reported
throughout.
Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ B.10 Held-out dev/test checkpoint-selection robustness ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
gives the triple-column comparison: all ten reported checkpoints lie
within $`\pm 1.85`$ pp (test$`-`$full), and dev selection reproduces the
checkpoints reported in the body under this split.

| Variant (step)                   | dev   | test  | full  | $`\Delta`$ |

### B.12 Response-period diagnostic interventions

Table [12](#A2.T12 "Table 12 ‣ B.12 Response-period diagnostic interventions ‣ Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
reports three diagnostic interventions on the same 200-question subset.
For informative failures, an empty response is replaced by a message
distinguishing “entity absent from the subgraph” from “relation
unavailable for this entity.” For two-call eligibility,
$`r_{\mathrm{retrv}}`$ is zero unless the trajectory contains at least
two distinct non-empty calls; all other interface and question content
is fixed.

| Intervention                       | Scope                | Result                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| R-toolverbs + informative failures | 2 seeds; $`n{=}200`$ | Peak EM $`37.0\%/36.5\%`$ versus $`34.0\%`$ for the matched diagnostic baseline.                                                                                                 |
| R-selfV + informative failures     | 2 seeds; $`n{=}200`$ | Both reach strict EM=$`0`$, CvT=$`0`$, Tools/Q$`\approx 1`$ by step 150. Messages alone do not prevent the cliff; added text also enters the quote-sensitive reward surface.     |
| R-selfV + two-call eligibility     | 3 seeds; $`n{=}200`$ | No baseline-time cliff through steps 300, 350, and 400; Tools/Q remains $`3.0`$ and CvT remains nonzero, identifying one-call eligibility as a causal lever over these horizons. |

Table 12: Diagnostic interventions for failure feedback and reward
eligibility. These 200-question runs resolve transition dynamics rather
than the full-test performance level.

## Appendix C SFT corpora

#### Rule-based shared SFT corpus (5,000 trajectories).

The shared SFT initialisation used by every reward variant is
constructed from the CWQ training split as follows. (i) For each
question, the gold triple chain is extracted from the WebQuestionsSP
annotation. (ii) \<think\> content is filled in from one of three fixed
templates with variable substitution (entities and relations drawn from
the gold chain). (iii) \<search\> calls are constructed directly from
the gold chain, with the tool response obtained by executing the query
against the Freebase sub-graph — so every call returns by construction a
response that contains the next entity on the gold path. (iv) The final
\<answer\> is the gold answer. _No LLM teacher is used anywhere in this
pipeline._

#### Enhanced variant (6,000 trajectories).

An enhanced variant sft_trajectories_enhanced.jsonl uses the same
pipeline with additional diversity in the \<think\> template and richer
tool-call ordering. Both corpora are used interchangeably for the shared
SFT base; results are not sensitive to which is used.

#### Self-distillation corpus (14,082 trajectories).

For init-from-iterate and self-distill
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested 40% band ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
we roll out the R-toolverbs·KL@400 checkpoint (HPC code: E5b-stab)
greedily on the full $`27{,}639`$-question CWQ training split, then
filter to trajectories satisfying _simultaneously_:

- •
  strict EM$`=1`$ against the normalised gold answer;
- •
  $`\geq 1`$ productive tool call (in the I-Self sense — non-empty
  response and $`\geq 1`$ returned entity in the final \<answer\>);
- •
  valid \<answer\> envelope format.

Yield: $`14{,}082`$ trajectories ($`50.9\%`$ of the $`27{,}639`$). This
corpus is LLM-generated but LLM-_self_-generated — no external teacher.

#### Methodological positioning.

Our shared SFT is teacher-free; the G-variant is self-distilled from our
own RL checkpoint. Both choices are deliberate.

## Appendix D GPT-4o closed-model schema-unfamiliarity control

We include a closed-model GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) baseline as a
_schema-unfamiliarity control_, not as a head-to-head comparator. The
substantive findings are GPT-4o’s $`\mathbf{6.2\%}`$ ContEM at $`1.46`$
tools/Q on $`n{=}500`$, with a 200-Q sub-evaluation showing
$`\sim 78\%`$ of trajectories self-describing as “unable to retrieve X”
(verbose-correct without strict gold-form match): a frontier closed
model under the same four-verb Freebase interface produces parseable
answers at near-$`100\%`$ format-validity, but retrieves little usable
content.

| Model                    | $`n`$ | EM                | ContEM | F1   | Tools/Q |
| ------------------------ | ----- | ----------------- | ------ | ---- | ------- |
| GPT-4o (5-shot ReAct)    | 500   | 0.6^($`\dagger`$) | 6.2    | 2.1  | 1.46    |
| R-stepwise @500 (ours)   | 3,531 | 32.5              | 45.3   | 38.1 | 1.00    |
| self-distill @500 (ours) | 3,531 | 40.0              | 49.5   | 42.8 | 3.00    |

Table 13: Closed-model schema-unfamiliarity control. All numbers are
percentages except $`n`$ and Tools/Q. The substantive GPT-4o findings
are the bolded ContEM $`6.2\%`$ and the low Tools/Q $`1.46`$ (vs.
self-distill’s $`3.00`$). ^($`\dagger`$)Strict EM reflects entity-casing
/ gold-form normalisation drift on closed-model output; ContEM is the
comparable metric for schema-unfamiliarity assessment.

#### Why we include this control.

Schema-unfamiliarity is a meaningful obstacle even at frontier
closed-model scale on this interface, so the $`\sim 10\%`$ CvT reached
by our trained models is not trivially dismissed as “the model is too
small”. The $`\sim 78\%`$ self-reported “unable to retrieve X” rate is
consistent with schema unfamiliarity as one obstacle, without isolating
it from reasoning ability.

#### Why this is a control, not a baseline.

GPT-4o is not RL-trained under our reward protocol and is evaluated
zero-shot, so we do not use it for head-to-head model ranking. Its role
is to contextualise the $`L_{\mathrm{lang}}`$ channel: a frontier closed
model without task-specific training also retrieves little under the
stripped interface.

## Appendix E Framework illustration and per-claim caveats

### E.1 Setup: standard multi-hop KGQA re-cast as a minimal tool interface

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: Setup: a standard multi-hop KGQA benchmark re-cast as a
minimal tool-use interface. CWQ questions over Freebase are reached by
composing four navigation verbs rather than by SPARQL or gold-subgraph
injection; entities are opaque machine IDs and an unsuccessful call
returns a bare \[\] — the two interface properties represented by
$`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ and $`L_{\mathrm{lang}}`$ in our framework
(§[5](#S5 "5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).

### E.2 Illustrative tool-family comparison

| Tool type    | Failure mode                            | Recovery signal       |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Python       | ZeroDivisionError                       | traceback (file:line) |
| Web search   | noisy but readable docs                 | extract anyway        |
| Function API | 400 + named param                       | fix parameter         |
| Browser/UI   | page state visible                      | DOM/visual            |
| KG tool      | wrong entity _or_ relation $`\to`$ \[\] | none                  |

Table 14: Illustrative failure and recovery signals across tool
families. In our stripped KG interface, a single empty-list response
cannot distinguish a wrong entity from a wrong relation or both,
motivating the $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ channel.

### E.3 Four-channel pathway diagram

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Four interface channels along the
policy $`\to`$ tool $`\to`$ reward pathway. Red dashed arrows mark
proposed locations of signal loss: $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$ (silent \[\]
responses), $`L_{\mathrm{lang}}`$ (opaque Freebase MIDs and dotted
relations), $`L_{\mathrm{comp}}`$ (entity IDs threaded across calls),
and $`L_{\mathrm{prior}}`$ (weak demonstrated prior for schema
navigation). Annotations connect the channels to observed failure modes
and intervention points.

### E.4 Per-claim caveats for P1–P4

P1–P4 are joint consistency checks of the descriptive framework; the
per-channel decomposition in
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Mechanism evidence chain ‣ 5 A Signal-Theoretic Account of Tool-Interface Difficulty ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")
(oracle intervention, behavioural diff, and decision-boundary analysis
on $`1{,}958`$ self-distill errors) provides the primary within-setting
evidence. The per-claim scope statements are:

- •
  P1 scope. R-binary/R-binary-SR format collapse evidences a joint
  $`L_{\mathrm{sig}}`$+$`L_{\mathrm{prior}}`$ degradation in the tested
  outcome-only setup.
- •
  P2 scope. The 7B self-distill and 14B R-toolverbs$`\cdot`$KL results
  use different reward recipes, making this a two-configuration
  comparison; a matched scaling run is the direct follow-up.
- •
  P3 scope. The init-from-iterate variant’s SFT is computed against a
  model already exposed to R-toolverbs·KL trajectories, so it absorbs
  less new signal per SFT step; the init-from-base ablation
  (§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Self-distillation: a one-iteration recipe reaches the tested 40% band ‣ 4 Results: A Reward Ladder Producing Four Failure Modes ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use"))
  isolates init source by removing the rule-based SFT pre-pass, with
  init-from-base $`\approx`$ self-distill $`\approx 40\%`$ EM
  establishing _sufficiency_ of init-from-base.
- •
  P4 scope. The KGQAGen-10k cross-benchmark Spearman $`\rho{=}0.976`$ is
  evaluated on _base_ Qwen variants, establishing transfer of base-model
  ordering; trained-policy transfer is the next comparison.

## Appendix F Cross-family boundary check: Llama-3.1-8B-Base

We apply the self-distill protocol to Llama-3.1-8B-Base, following
Search-R1’s model choice for a multi-turn verl-based setup ([Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)); the 8B-Instruct variant’s tool-use limitations are
documented in Meta’s model card. Pipeline, hyperparameters, and SFT
corpus match the Qwen self-distill setting
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C SFT corpora ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
Because the reward differs from R-selfV, this is a cross-family boundary
check rather than a matched replication of the Qwen cliff.

| Stage         | EM                 | Tools/Q           | Tool-involving |
| ------------- | ------------------ | ----------------- | -------------- |
| SFT-only      | $`0.284`$          | $`0.65`$          | $`44.4\%`$     |
| GRPO step 50  | $`0.327`$          | $`\mathbf{0.00}`$ | $`0.1\%`$      |
| GRPO step 100 | $`\mathbf{0.345}`$ | $`\mathbf{0.00}`$ | $`0.0\%`$      |

Table 15: Llama-3.1-8B-Base on full CWQ test ($`n{=}3531`$).
“Tool-involving” = share of trajectories with $`\geq 1`$ tool call under
the 7-category classifier
(App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reward formulas and trajectory classifier ‣ Peak-Then-Collapse and the Four Interface Channels ofKnowledge-Graph Tool Use")).
Wilson 95% CIs $`\pm 1.6`$ pp at $`n{=}3531`$.

#### Cross-architecture interpretation.

Llama-Base GRPO reaches EM=$`0.345`$ at step 100 versus Qwen
self-distill’s $`0.400`$ at step 500, but exhibits a qualitatively
distinct collapse: Tools/Q drops to $`0`$ by step 50 and SFT-only’s
$`44.4\%`$ tool-involving share falls to approximately $`0\%`$. The
policy becomes purely parametric ($`32.5\%`$ correct-no-tool $`+`$
$`67.5\%`$ wrong-no-tool), unlike the Qwen/R-selfV quote-and-stop
trajectory. The contrast motivates a matched cross-family experiment.
